column2: Silver buses float above the city without wheels or roads, and blue lights show their way between the tallest glass buildings.
All the houses are grey and have the same number, and a camera follows each child who walks towards the school.
Behind the thick window on the ship's quiet upper floor, two orange moons rise over a dark and empty planet.
At the far end of the station's empty platform, a tall man moves each time I take a step.
The little robot carries tea across the moon base kitchen, and its round green eyes flash when it finds my cup.
Red flowers of light open above the dark roofs, and my brother laughs and covers both his small ears.
Hot cars fill the road from end to end, and a dog watches us from an open window.
Tiny cars move along the roads far below me, and the buildings look like boxes in the bright sun.
Our light finds wet leaves above the narrow path, and insects make a loud song in the dark trees.
The little fields hold the last red evening light, and a farmer walks slowly down the steps between them.
Thin white mist floats above the slow brown river, and a bird calls loudly from the trees along the bank.
Green leaves make soft shadows across the narrow road, and a little bird hops along the warm stone wall.
Moonlight makes a white square on the empty classroom floor, and a small coat hangs alone beside the closed wooden door.
Big wheels turn slowly inside the old stone tower, and each loud tick makes the wooden floor shake under us.
Green fields flash past the window faster than I can count, and a little house appears and disappears behind the dark trees.
Our boat moves slowly past gardens behind the sleeping houses, and warm light shines from a kitchen above the quiet water.
Empty chairs stand behind the closed gates of the pier, and cold wind moves a torn sign above the dark café.
White flowers lean over plates with food still on them, and a cleaner lifts bright ribbons from the long red carpet.
The loud bell rings above the fire station's red doors, and boots hit the floor as people run towards the engines.
Lanterns glow like little suns above the crowded festival street, and people lift their children higher to see the moving lights.
Brown leaves gather at the bottom of the empty pool, and cold wind pushes another one across the bright blue tiles.
Inside the little box behind the shop's broken clock, a new key lies beside a map of our street.
The teacher's chair gives a loud squeak whenever she moves, and the class looks down quickly and tries not to laugh.
Beside the snowy cliff high above the empty valley, a red flag moves against the sky like a hand.
The old map lies flat on a warm grey stone, and a line of footprints leads away through the yellow grass.
Snow covers the ground outside the small locked cabin, and one fresh flower lies on the table beside the fire.
Inside the narrow tunnel beneath the broken castle wall, cold air touches our faces from somewhere far ahead.
Behind the mirror in the room above the station, someone has written tomorrow's date in bright red paint.
Beside the big sign at the front of the gym, a tired man eats cake under words about healthy living.
Beneath the market's last few yellow lights, a tired man counts coins into a small box.
Below the huge red signs along the street, two sisters compare their bags and start to laugh.
Inside the little shop by the empty road, a man reads a book beside warm coffee cups.
On the hard seats inside the small bus station, a family sleeps beside bags tied with red string.
Between the tall green stems beside the wet path, a patch of sunlight shines on the soft brown ground.
On the wet stones beside the falling water, tiny plants shake under drops as cold as ice.
Under the burnt branches near the edge of the forest, our shoes leave dark marks in the soft grey ash.
Under the bright lights beside the hospital's closed doors, a paper cup stands cold on an empty blue chair.
Inside a blue book on the shop's narrow table, a dry brown leaf rests between two pages of poems.
Between the empty chairs in the little late-night laundry, a single red sock lies alone on the white floor.
Near the back of the cinema before the lights fade, two friends whisper and hide their phones inside their coats.
Beside the fishing boats under the pale new morning sky, birds wait on wooden posts and watch the open boxes.
Inside the busy temple beside the tall gold statue, a little girl holds flowers with both her small hands.
At the busy water's edge beside the crowded summer beach, a small boy laughs as waves wash over his feet.
Between the wet buckets in the busy festival flower market, a man wraps pink flowers in a sheet of white paper.
Under a small lamp inside the quiet grey submarine, green lines move across a screen beside a sleeping man.
Women carry water from the stone well beside the church, and horses pull heavy carts along the town's muddy main street.
From the silent garden door, where his clean red boots still stand, I can see the little swing he loved hanging still above the grass.
Under the little bed in the quiet locked room, something is taking a breath whenever I stop taking my own.
Beneath the smoking lamps inside the old printing room, a boy is putting small metal letters into a wooden tray.
Under the bridge at the end of the king's garden, a frog is wearing a crown much brighter than the stars.
On the table beside the meal she will never eat, a cup is growing cold with her lipstick on its edge.
When the steam train arrives in a cloud of smoke, a soldier lifts his small sister above the waiting crowd.
A bright plastic chair floats past our gate on the brown water covering the road.
Our neighbour brings a chair outside and smiles, and candles glow in windows along the dark street.
Beside a big round pot full of white steam, a woman fills paper bags with soft hot dumplings.
Above the rubbish hill, white birds turn in circles over a torn blue bag on the high fence.
Below the distant hills, hot air makes the far end of the straight black road move like water.
Green tea plants make straight lines across the wet ground, and mist hides the tops of the hills beyond us.
Outside the small circle our torch makes on the rock, the darkness feels very big.
People pull cloth over their faces and close their doors against the thick clouds of brown sand moving through the town.
Over the scrape of chairs and the children's laughter, someone taps out a quick rhythm on the nearest wooden desk.
Above the hiss of hot pans, a man shouts the next order to the cooks rushing past each other.
In the last light of the day, a cleaner pushes her bucket past the museum's huge stone lion and across the long empty room.
Small green birds hop between sticks above a white rabbit eating slowly from a blue plastic bowl in the pet shop window.
On the softly rocking night train, a little reading light shines behind the thin blue curtain of a narrow bed.
One worker sweeps the paper cups from the steps of the empty stadium into a slowly growing white pile.
Behind the small door inside the baker's warm shop, a staircase is climbing between clouds towards a bright green moon.
Beside the school gate on my first morning alone, my new jacket seems too big across my narrow shoulders.
A black cat with very wide gold eyes watches the girl's shadow leave her feet and climb the wall.
The little wall no longer reaches as high as my waist, and our childhood hiding place is open to the evening sky.
Beside the empty glass case in the locked museum, a dark glove is lying on the clean white floor.
Across the wide valley beyond the ruins of our village, another small fire is sending thin grey smoke into the sky.
Inside the glass tower above the dark sleeping forest, a boy is keeping winter in a little wooden box.
Under the short pencil marks beside our kitchen door, my little sister is standing straight and asking me to measure.
Beside a red door in the narrow street, a woman is warming her hands around a steaming cup.
On the white path beside the frozen flowers, our footprints form a dark line towards the gate.
Beneath the tall crane at the quiet building site, a white hat is lying upside down on a wall.
Below the purple sky at the edge of the playground, a small red ball is resting in the dark grass.
Near the snowy bank under the brightening winter sky, tiny bubbles form white lines inside the hard ice.
Under the clear water beside the high coral wall, a blue fish is waiting in a dark little hole.
Between the fruit trees in the warm autumn light, wooden boxes hold fresh apples with a sweet warm smell.
Outside our classroom on the last day of school, a teacher is taking the colourful pictures down from the wall.
Beneath the little window at the top of the house, sunlight is showing the dust on a pile of old photographs.
Inside the little lift between the dark silent floors, a man is holding his shopping bags against his shaking knees.
Beside the closed ticket office on the crowded platform, a woman is sitting on her case and sharing her biscuits.
Between the silver sides of the station's moving stairs, a small child is holding a hand and watching each step.
Under the big tree beside the village wedding tables, children are throwing white flower petals over a smiling young couple.
Beside the school stage behind the closed red curtain, a teacher is giving quiet smiles to children with shaking hands.
Under the big tree in the quiet misty graveyard, rainwater is filling the letters on one small pale stone.
A black dress hangs alone beside the tall stone fireplace, and rain streaks the windows above the mansion's deserted entrance hall.
Her scarlet scarf rests beside mine across the small café table, and our wet hands touch briefly as we reach for warm cups.
The missing button on his worn coat, which still hangs beside mine behind the kitchen door, reminds me of all his busy mornings.
In the blowing dust outside the frontier town's wooden bank, a brown horse stands under a loudly squeaking sign.
Beneath the ruined tower beyond the ancestral house's neglected gardens, white roses grow around a stone with no clear name.
Beneath the garden's oldest tree beyond the crowded afternoon party, he waits with two chairs and the book I lost.
At a bus stop outside the shuttered neighbourhood florist, a woman holds fresh oranges and looks down the empty road.
She laughs at the flour dusting my face and sleeves, and the kitchen seems warmer when she stands close beside me.
In the emptied flat, each footstep comes back with an unfamiliar brightness from walls marked with pale squares where our pictures used to hang.
Our footsteps echo between rows of sleeping concrete pillars, and a green light shines beside the only open door.
Holding their coats closed, people step around deep puddles full of rippling pink reflections.
Children wave paper flowers and dance beside the road to drums thundering beneath the bright flags of the procession.
Sunflowers lower their heavy heads over the heat-baked field in a hot wind that brings no relief.
Tired students drink water and rub their eyes before reading, and open textbooks occupy every available corner of the library tables.
Fresh loaves crowd the shelves behind the bakery's darkened window, and a baker puts another tray into the hot bright oven.
When green foam spills over the rim of the beaker onto the laboratory bench, our teacher reaches for towels and tells us to step back.
Cups slide across the table beside my mother's wet gloves, and grey waves strike the ferry beneath its shuddering passenger lounge.
Container ships wait beside towering stacks of red and blue cargo, and tall cranes move slowly above them like very big birds.
Grandma laughs at the family squeezing more chairs around a table crowded with red bowls and steaming dishes.
Weeds spread across the deserted theme park's once crowded paths, and a bright dragon smiles above a closed and broken gate.
Small fish drift through the wreck's shattered bridge windows and over cups half-buried in soft sand.
Beneath the orbital city's crowded network of artificial streets, huge warm machines make the air that everyone must breathe.
Behind the stairwell door above the building's silent lower floors, slow footsteps stop whenever I stop breathing in the dark.
Behind the security gate inside the town's regulated public park, one small flower grows beside a sign that says no.
A red dot moves slowly across the wall beside me, and the lift opens onto a floor without a single working light.
The kitchen display assigns each household its daily public score, and warm water comes only when our number is high enough.
Across the rain-swept bridge above the evening's slow-moving traffic, a woman runs while looking back at every passing car.
Inside the silent café behind the city's highest security wall, rich people drink without screens calling out their names.
At the evening signal, the city's adaptive towers rearrange themselves above us and close their windows like eyes.
Someone has moved my bag from my chair to the floor in the few minutes since my screen went dark.
Uniformed children advance through the school gates in rigid rows, and a girl hides a bright ribbon inside her closed hand.
On the automated planet's unlit hemisphere beyond the landing zone, small white lights move in rows without any human hands.
Along the deserted street after the compulsory evening announcement, doors close together like books nobody is allowed to read.
Beside the rooftop wall beneath the New Year fireworks, we watch green light fall slowly through the smoke.
Between motionless vehicles in the thick afternoon heat, a man sells cold water from a blue bag.
Beside a black stream beneath the rainforest's hidden canopy, two small green eyes shine back towards our little light.
Along curved terrace walls above the deepening valley shadows, water shines in rows like steps towards the evening sky.
Between shadowed jungle banks in the first uncertain daylight, our little boat leaves a silver line in the water.
Beside a quiet lane beneath the still summer sky, yellow flowers grow around a gate with peeling blue paint.
Between silent desks beneath the classroom's dark windowpanes, a red pencil lies beside a book of unfinished work.
Around the flour-dusted table in my grandmother's crowded kitchen, we roll soft dough while she tells us old stories.
On the low table inside the dentist's quiet waiting room, old magazines lie beside a toy with one broken wheel.
Behind the clock face high above the town square, daylight shines through numbers much taller than my little brother.
Beside the narrowboat in the canal's cool early light, a duck swims through the steam from our warm breakfast.
Beneath dimmed chandeliers inside the wedding hall's sudden emptiness, two gold shoes wait together under a red velvet chair.
When the alarm sounds in the fire station, blue lights flash across the walls and the waiting red engines.
Beneath red lanterns near the packed festival's narrow entrance, a girl protects her paper fish from the passing crowd.
Beside the observation window high above the planet's blue curve, a little photograph of my family floats against the wall.
Of the three cups on a table with only two chairs, one retains a warmth the empty house cannot explain.
The dog wears a hat that completely conceals its ears; its owner conducts an increasingly indignant search around the living room.
Beneath the mayor's portrait inside the town hall's crowded reception, a misplaced umbrella transforms the mayor's nose into a dripping beak.
Beside the washing machine inside our otherwise ordinary family kitchen, a small raincloud awaits its customary release through the back door.
Below the island's shadowed cliff, where our boat scrapes the rocks, a cave mouth holds a light nobody expected to find.
The king's oversized robe trails behind him like a carpet; a mouse occupies the crown with substantially greater confidence.
Once the final customers have drifted towards the darkening entrance, a market vendor gathers the evening into folds of faded cloth.
Shoppers in the patient queue curling around windows bright with advertisements rehearse their purchases with lists clenched like boarding passes.
Two petrol pumps glow beside the otherwise deserted highway; the surrounding landscape absorbs the light without revealing its edges.
The driver of a solitary bus idling beneath the station's tired yellow lamps lingers over a cup of tea beside the shuttered office.
Each drop ticking from the bamboo's slender leaves acquires an improbable clarity in the enclosed stillness of the grove.
The unbroken roar of white water plunging between the gorge's steep dark walls leaves almost no room for human speech.
Storm-torn seaweed marks the beach in uneven brown ribbons; a splintered branch shares the sand with an immaculate blue bucket.
A single green shoot among the charred trees makes the devastation of the ash-covered forest floor newly visible.
Above a weary mother tucking a coat around her sleeping child, the station clock maintains a precision nobody finds remotely comforting.
With complete authority, a sleeping cat has claimed an unsorted carton beneath the bookshop's crowded wooden shelves.
Beneath the blank screen, the rustle of popcorn in the slowly filling seats establishes the audience's first collective soundtrack.
Dawn brushes the fishing boats moored along the wet harbour wall; a fisher draws another length of net from a tangled heap.
On a beach covered in overlapping towels and umbrellas, children negotiate the temporary frontiers between families with dripping buckets and absolute confidence.
Along the festival market's narrow street, customers lower their faces towards buckets of bright flowers as though the blooms might offer advice.
Ruined castle walls rise above the restless dark coastal water; seabirds enter windows from which human observers have long disappeared.
A crew member turns sideways to squeeze between bunks and suspended clothing in the submarine's pipe-crowded passage.
Inside the castle kitchen beside its enormous soot-darkened hearth, a kitchen boy tends the roasting meat with exhausted concentration.
Long after the farewells have become inaudible, a passenger's white handkerchief keeps waving from the rail of the departing merchant vessel.
The millwheel turns despite the stream's long and dusty silence; moonlight collects as flour beneath the old miller's patient hands.
Inside the stalled lift after its final bulb flickers out, someone pronounces my name with breath cold enough to hurt.
The watchmen lift lanterns to inspect the rain-darkened uniform of a mounted messenger beneath the city's heavy timber gateway.
Beside the black lake below the abandoned hospital's empty windows, a submerged bell begins the familiar summons for visiting hour.
On the shop steps above the drifting floodwater, two neighbours exchange the morning's news over carefully balanced tea.
Beside the powerless traffic signals at the darkened crossroads, a baker directs the hesitant traffic with his floury hand.
Beside the dumpling stall in the sharp morning cold, a schoolboy breathes the rising steam before taking his first bite.
Among crushed boxes along the dump's windblown outer fence, one yellow flower occupies the fractured seat of a plastic chair.
Beneath the cave's low ceiling beside its dripping wall, our shadows expand into enormous figures at the torch's slightest movement.
Inside a shuttered shop beside the storm-darkened market street, an untouched glass of tea gradually acquires a delicate sandy rim.
Beneath harsh kitchen lights behind the restaurant's swinging doors, a chef positions one delicate leaf with almost absurd precision.
Behind locked glass doors in the museum's empty evening galleries, reflected faces hover beside masks whose original wearers nobody remembers.
Under a bright canopy amid the floating market's crowded boats, a vendor steadies the soup with the ease of long experience.
Below the dark scoreboard beside the stadium's deserted pitch, one forgotten scarf maintains a small defiant patch of colour.
Under a faded sign beside the fairground's frozen ticket kiosk, one torn streamer continues a thin and solitary winter dance.
Inside the faded bedroom beyond the house's broken staircase, a hanging dress preserves the suggestion of someone about to return.
Before the bank's damaged frontage, which breaks the emergency lights into jagged fragments, an evidence bag gives ordinary coins an unfamiliar ceremonial importance.
Within a hollow older than the village's earliest remembered name, a cobbler repairs shoes whose golden soles have never touched earth.
Beneath interview lights designed to eliminate every inconvenient patch of shadow, a recovered watch gleams beside coffee abandoned during an abrupt confession.
From the forced door, an untidy frame for the otherwise immaculate storeroom, oily tracks lead towards a street the rain has almost washed clean.
In the unchanged kitchen, where I suddenly feel like an unfamiliar version of myself, my father's patient silence offers a responsibility more disconcerting than permission.
A departing worker sheds the day's weight in flakes of mud beneath the angular silhouettes of the machinery.
Sunrise stains the frozen lake with colour almost too delicate to name; an imprisoned branch remains suspended beneath the crystalline surface.
Sunlight redraws its restless lattice across the bare sand around a reef sheltering a quicksilver multitude of fish.
A picker tests each apple on the heavily laden branches with an almost conversational touch.
The corridor overflows with a term's worth of released impatience; a paper aeroplane sails magnificently above the departing backpacks.
Clipped hair gathers into a dark provisional shadow beneath the chair of a barber who punctuates his conversation with swift flashes of silver.
The platform's accumulated impatience finds a focus in the flickering board; each revised arrival time releases another small wave of disbelief.
Shoulders brushing on the crowded escalator towards the daylight never quite interrupt the privacy of anyone's thoughts.
The rotating beam briefly exposes a sea apparently determined to climb the lighthouse's storm-battered stones.
The rink organises its evening crowd into overlapping loops of movement; a beginner negotiates the wall with fierce and unsmiling determination.
Amid the whispered instructions and compulsively adjusted costumes backstage, one young performer examines his hat as though it contains the answer.
A rook maintains its solitary watch above the rusting gate of a graveyard whose mist conceals the ends of its narrow paths.
Within a gallery whose shutters have excluded decades of ordinary daylight, a disused piano offers its yellowed keys to the damp.
Under a coat insufficient for two people determined to share it, we watch the boats return without discussing our own departure.
In the narrow space between the draining board and the wall, a spoon maintains the position her absent hand once gave it.
Within a church whose roof remains more intention than accomplished shelter, wind distributes prairie dust across the carpenters' carefully stacked new pews.
The tide revisits the house with the persistence of an inherited grievance; the family silver trembles inside its cabinet with each returning assault.
In a conversation circling subjects too small to accommodate what remains unsaid, the cooling tea becomes the only change neither of us can prevent.
Among travellers whose competing departures should make recognition almost impossible, his smile reaches me before his raised hand clears the crowd.
Among shelves whose familiar arrangement makes the intervening years seem implausible, the shopkeeper remembers my childhood purchase with embarrassing exactness.
Within the store's narrow strip of shade beyond the sun-bleached hitching rail, a saddler restores usefulness to leather polished by years of distance.
Long after the final sentence, her finger still guards a page in the finished book that she no longer needs to find.
Past iron gates whose elaborate initials nobody now troubles to decipher, the ancestral house emerges above trees darkened almost beyond green.
Beneath the bookshop awning, our shoulders stay pressed together long after the easing rain has stopped making it necessary.
Beyond a gate whose familiar catch now opens for somebody else, flowers occupy a chipped cup I had forgotten leaving behind.
Through the market's mingled scents of seawater and crushed herbs, a porter shoulders baskets that trail droplets like loose beads.
Beneath a ceiling crowded with colour-coded pipes and ducts, a puddle holds an immaculate miniature of the fluorescent lights.
Beneath lettering whose electric blue stains the descending rain, a late customer scatters luminous droplets from her soaked coat.
Borne above the procession on poles hidden by moving bodies, a painted fish swims magnificently through the city's ordinary air.
Within the palm grove's abruptly cooler enclosure of green shade, our dust-covered luggage looks strangely misplaced against the tender grass.
Beneath limestone pinnacles whose abrupt shapes dominate the river valley, a riverside dwelling seems almost provisional beside the patient rock.
Among sunflowers whose bowed heads seem incapable of further resistance, the soil opens into fissures around each stubborn upright stem.
Within the reading lamp's concentrated circle of almost theatrical brightness, a student rehearses one definition until its meaning feels unfamiliar.
Among floor markings that remember competition conducted at a different speed, an invigilator places sealed questions on each isolated island of wood.
From a lounge whose furniture has acquired an unfamiliar restlessness, we watch spray erase the horizon in successive white convulsions.
Among vessels whose enormous sides conceal their far-flung commercial journeys, a yellow truck transfers another steel parcel towards the waiting city.
Within the coach's shifting geography of friendship and exchanged snacks, two pupils divide a packet of sweets with diplomatic precision.
Where the amplifiers have fallen silent and the crowds have scattered, a pair of glittering boots remains planted firmly in the mud.
Within the familiar circle renewed by another Lunar New Year, a child's careful hands confer enormous importance on a small red envelope.
Beyond a café window whose cheerful lettering has begun to peel, dust settles indiscriminately across tables reserved for nobody at all.
